 By Brad Biggs | bmbiggs@chicagotribune.com | Chicago Tribune PUBLISHED: November 15, 2026 at 6:00 AM CST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... The Chicago Bears made the most seismic move in recent weeks with the acquisition of Jeffery Simmons , and the division rival Minnesota Vikings created the biggest headlines at the NFL trade deadline by bringing back quarterback Kirk Cousins .
 Related Articles
 Are the Chicago Bears the NFC favorite? 5 pressing questions for the 2nd half of the season. 
 With some fixes, Chicago Bears ‘can really, really make a run at it.’ Here’s what else we heard at Halas Hall. 
 Chicago Bears win their 4th straight game to head into the bye week at 7-2: Brad Biggs’ 10 thoughts on Week 9 
 The NFC North is a gauntlet, and with nine weeks remaining in the regular season, it could be the most fascinating division race the league has seen in years.
 The Bears are atop the standings at 7-2 in their bye week, but the Vikings (6-2 and visiting the Green Bay Packers) and Detroit Lions (6-2 and playing the New England Patriots in Germany) can match that record with victories Sunday. For all of their early-season issues, the Packers have won five of six to reach 6-3, and they stand to improve in the near future with edge rusher Micah Parsons close to returning from the torn ACL he suffered last season.
 The four NFC North teams are a combined 20-4 against non-division opponents. Two of those losses were to the Buffalo Bills, who defeated the Lions and Vikings. The North teams’ 25-9 overall record (.735 winning percentage) is the best for one division through nine weeks in league history. The NFC East was at .727 through nine weeks in 2002.
 Since the league was aligned into eight four-team divisions in 2002, no division has produced four playoff teams. It didn’t become possible until 2020, when the NFL expanded to a 14-team playoff format with three wild cards from each conference.
 Statistically, it’s possible the NFC North could send its champion and three wild-card teams to the postseason. Based on the current standings, it would happen. With so much time remaining in the season, it’s premature to speculate on the possibility. How the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Rams, both 5-4, fare will be a factor in how many North teams reach the tournament.
 The North teams probably would have to split most of their division games to make it more feasible. If a team tanks in the division with, say, a 1-5 record, it would be more difficult to seize the seventh and final seed. According to ESPN, entering Week 10 all four teams have a greater than 60% chance of making the playoffs.
 Last season the Bears became only the fourth team since the NFL-AFL merger in 1970 to win a division title while finishing below .500 against its division. Considering how rare that is, it’s unlikely the North champion repeats the feat.
 Sizing up the NFC North race at the midway point.
 Chicago Bears (7-2, 0-2 in division)
 Bears defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons (99) helps on a tackle in the fourth quarter against the Buccaneers on Nov. 8, 2026, at Soldier Field. (John J. Kim/Chicago Tribune) 
 The addition of Simmons, a true multiplier for Dennis Allen’s defense , gives the Bears a chance to remain a top-10 defense in many key metrics. They are No. 1 on third down (22.8%) and rank in the top 10 in total defense, rushing yards allowed per game, interception rate, sacks per pass play and points allowed.
 The defense was playing relatively well to this point last season before some elements, especially third-down success, plummeted. That’s unlikely to happen with Simmons, who should have equal impact on the pass rush — the Bears are No. 3 in sacks per pass play — and run defense.
 The degree of difficulty gets ratcheted up. Four of the remaining eight games are against teams that are in the top five in scoring (the Bills, Jacksonville Jaguars and Lions twice), and the Vikings (27th) and Miami Dolphins (31st) are the only remaining opponents outside of the top half.
 Allen will be able to pick and choose spots to blitz more with Simmons and won’t have to lean so heavily on five- and six-man rushes to generate pressure while risking big plays on the back end.
 With quarterback Caleb Williams experienced in so many late fourth-quarter comebacks, the Bears have confidence in their ability to close out games, just as they did Sunday night against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
 Detroit Lions (6-2, 2-0)
 Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs runs against the Dolphins on Nov. 8, 2026, in Miami Gardens, Fla. (AP Photo/Doug Murray) 
 A 2-0 start in the division was key, considering three of the Lions’ final four games are trips to Minnesota (Week 15), Chicago (Week 17) and Green Bay (Week 18).
 Dan Campbell’s high-powered offense will have to prove it can remain formidable in cold weather and potentially poor conditions. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs leads the NFL with 177 carries, just 73 shy of his career high of 250, and he’s on pace for 448 touches. Only six running backs in NFL history have had more in a season, a list topped by the Bucs’ James Wilder in 1984 (492 — 407 carries, 85 receptions).
 That’s a massive workload for the 5-foot-9, 202-pound Gibbs and makes it fair to question how he will hold up as the season wears on. But bigger questions remain for a defense that has rushed the quarterback well (third in the NFL with 27 sacks) but gets hit by too many big plays, including a league-high 34 pass plays for 20 or more yards.
 The return of safety Brian Branch has helped, and the Lions hope safety Kerby Joseph returns soon. Better communication on the back end should prevent so many breakdowns in coverage, but like the Bears, the Lions are not great at cornerback.
 Minnesota Vikings (6-2, 2-1)
 Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins listens to a question during a news conference Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, in Eagan, Minn. (John Autey/St. Paul Pioneer Press) 
 The Vikings had to do something at quarterback, and that was evident before the Bills pulled away Monday night in a game in which the Minnesota offense simply couldn’t compete against a poorly ranked Buffalo defense.
 The Vikings have scored only 11 offensive touchdowns through eight games (the Bears have 27 in nine games), and five came in the season-opening blowout of the Packers at Lambeau Field. Wide receiver Justin Jefferson caught eight passes for 92 yards and two touchdowns in that game. In six games he has played since, he has 23 catches for 301 yards and two touchdowns. That’s a nice two-week stretch for Jefferson when the offense is cooking.
 Enter Cousins, 38, who was acquired from the Las Vegas Raiders for a third-round pick, another trade that could have a substantial impact on the playoffs. Cousins has 20 touchdown passes, trailing only the Cincinnati Bengals’ Joe Burrow (23), and he did that in a Las Vegas offense that hasn’t been able to run the ball at all and has Tre Tucker and Jalen Nailor as its top wideouts.
 The question is how long it will take Cousins to get re-acclimated to coach Kevin O’Connell’s offense. The Vikings don’t need to be an offensive juggernaut to be very dangerous. If they can have a league-average offense in the second half — and Cousins’ presence should breath some life into a listless running game — they will be a tough out.
 The Vikings are happy to turn a game into an alley fight and lean on Brian Flores’ formidable defense. They close the season by hosting the Bears in Week 18 after playing the Washington Commanders (3-5-1) and New York Jets (2-7) in Weeks 16 and 17.
 Green Bay Packers (6-3, 1-2)
 Packers running back Josh Jacobs (8) reacts with quarterback Jordan Love (10) and wide receiver Matthew Golden (0) after scoring a touchdown against the Panthers on Oct. 29, 2026, in Green Bay. (AP Photo/Jeffrey Phelps) 
 Sunday’s game against the Vikings has huge stakes for the Packers, who would fall two games back in the loss column to the Bears and Vikings — and potentially the Lions — with a loss. It’s one of only two NFC North games (the other being Bears at Lions on Thanksgiving) before Week 15.
 The Packers are leaning on a vertical passing game with quarterback Jordan Love and receivers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, and they lead the NFL in passes of 20-plus and 40-plus yards. That has made up for a putrid running game that is averaging a league-low 68.2 yards per game and 3.04 yards per carry (31st). Running back Josh Jacobs hasn’t looked good when he has played, and now he’s sidelined with a broken finger.
 Defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon has gotten strong results in his first season. Green Bay is second in the league with 19 takeaways, and things stand to improve when Parsons finally gets back on the field.
 The Packers’ hopes hinge on somehow finding a way to run the ball more effectively behind an offensive line that had a host of issues and injuries at the start of the season. It’s really difficult for an offense to hold up behind a patchwork O-line over the course of a season. Love’s steady hand has had the Packers on a roll, and they will go as far as he can carry them.
 Stakes are high and there will be massive implications at the end of the year. The Bears schedule ends with home games against the Packers and Lions and a trip to Minneapolis. A first-round bye might be key for the North winner to advance in the playoffs, considering how grueling the stretch run will be.
 Right now the San Francisco 49ers are No. 1 in the NFC at 7-1. With three NFC North teams a good bet to reach the playoffs — and maybe even all four — the divisional storyline likely will play out into the postseason.
